title: What can we do if it turns out that the Secretary of State for Education doesn't believe in education?
author: Old, Andrew
summary: Responding to England's newly appointed Education Secretary posting that 'an over-focus on academic outcomes has left too many young people behind,' this piece treats the statement as a potential signal of hostility toward academic, knowledge-rich education from within the traditionalist camp the author has belonged to for over a decade. Rather than organized protest, the author's prescribed response is explicitly grassroots and individual: keep teaching well regardless of political headwinds, stick to evidence-based principles (phonics, cognitive-science-grounded instruction) regardless of which way the political wind blows, and maintain a public or pseudonymous voice for sharing ideas even without official institutional support. The piece situates its argument historically, noting the 2000s-2010s traditionalist movement succeeded without a formal leader or government backing, simply through teachers sharing ideas with each other, and that no single politician — good or bad — has ever managed to fully reshape English education policy within a single term of office. The closing message is a form of professional resilience: 'muddle through, don't give up, don't sell out, don't wait for politicians to get it right,' framed as advice for surviving a possible ideological reversal without abandoning either one's job or one's convictions.
points: The immediate trigger is a public statement from England's new Education Secretary — 'an over-focus on academic outcomes has left too many young people behind' — read as a possible signal of renewed hostility to knowledge-rich, academic education.
The prescribed response is deliberately grassroots rather than organized protest: 'the priority is not protesting or setting up a rebel alliance against the empire,' but returning to basics.

The historical parallel drawn is that the 2000s-2010s traditionalist education movement succeeded without any formal leader or government backing — 'it was mainly just teachers sharing ideas' anonymously online.
A concrete resilience strategy is offered for a harsher political climate: maintaining a pseudonymous or anonymous public voice if speaking openly under one's own name becomes professionally risky.

The closing frame is structural optimism about policy durability: 'no government has maintained a consistent direction in education policy for their whole term of office,' meaning even hostile politicians historically fail to fully implement sweeping reversals.
quotes: 'We must recognise that an over-focus on academic outcomes has left too many young people behind.'

If it isn't, I'd like to see some evidence for that as soon as possible. If it is, then having someone who is genuinely indifferent to, or even hostile to, academic achievement would be a disaster for the education system and probably not what the public wants either.
Teach. This is the reason for everything... I will be standing at the front showing kids how to do maths until they sack me or kill me.
Stick to your principles. What works hasn't changed, and none of us will easily forget that we saw it working... There is a science of learning. Phonics works.
The traditionalist movement of the late 2000s and early 2010s was not led by Michael Gove or Nick Gibb. It didn't really have a leader. It was mainly just teachers sharing ideas with teachers.
Muddle through. Don't give up. Don't sell out. Don't wait for politicians to get it right.
